entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Battista Agnese (died 1564), a seminal cartographer originating from the Republic of Genoa, established his influential workshop in the Venetian Republic during the first half of the 16th century. His meticulous manuscript atlases, produced between approximately 1535 and 1564, represent a pinnacle of portolan chart tradition at a time of burgeoning global exploration, offering some of the most beautiful and accurate navigational aids of the era. His work bridged the practical demands of Mediterranean and Atlantic shipping with the artistic flourishes characteristic of Renaissance craftsmanship, making him a central figure in the dissemination of geographical knowledge across Europe.

Agnese's workshop was prolific, producing at least 71 known atlases, a remarkable output for a period dominated by hand-drawn maps. These exquisite works typically contained 10-12 charts, often including a world map on an oval projection (like the cordiform or polar projection), regional charts of the Mediterranean, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans, and celestial spheres. He was among the first to depict the route of Ferdinand Magellan's circumnavigation of the globe (1519–1522) and to include details of the Gulf of California, reflecting the most current geographical discoveries emanating from Spanish and Portuguese expeditions. His charts, often commissioned by wealthy merchants and nobles, were not merely navigational tools but also status symbols and sources of strategic information.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Battista Agnese's prolific output of exquisite portolan atlases significantly advanced the visual representation of global geography during the Age of Exploration, influencing subsequent cartographic practice. His works provided crucial navigational and strategic information, shaping European understanding of a rapidly expanding world.
